title: Quantum error correction at ultra-low overhead
authors: Zhide Lu, Weikang Li, Dong-Ling Deng
abstract: Suppressing errors is the central challenge for useful large-scale quantum computing. While quantum error correction promises a viable solution to this challenge, existing codes typically suffer from trade-offs among encoding efficiency, error threshold, and hardware feasibility. Here, we introduce Cornucopia codes, a family of practical, hardware-efficient quantum low-density parity-check codes that achieve an ultra-high encoding rate exceeding $1/2$ while maintaining a pseudo-threshold exceeding $0.4\%$ under the standard circuit-level noise model. Inspired by recent affine-permutation-based code constructions and the long-range connectivity available in reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays, we adopt a structured code geometry in which the code layout, atom rearrangement, and syndrome-extraction schedule are co-designed. This structure enables nonlocal syndrome measurements through simple, parallel atom rearrangements. A complete syndrome extraction cycle measures all $X$- and $Z$-type checks in parallel with $12$ entangling layers, independent of the code size. The resulting threshold is comparable to those of the surface code and bivariate bicycle codes. In particular, a single code block $[[2844,1426,18]]$ encodes $1{,}426$ distance-$18$ logical qubits, achieving an extrapolated logical error rate of $2.6\times10^{-16}$ ($1.9\times10^{-31}$) per logical qubit per cycle, assuming the physical error rate of $0.1\%$ ($0.01\%$). By comparison, a bivariate bicycle code implementation would require more than $68{,}000$ physical qubits to encode the same number of logical qubits at a comparable logical error rate. These results bring demonstrations of ultra-low overhead quantum error correction within the reach of near-term quantum processors.
summary: This paper introduces Cornucopia codes, a new family of quantum error correcting codes designed specifically for implementation on neutral-atom arrays. These codes overcome traditional trade-offs by achieving high encoding rates and robust error thresholds while maintaining low physical overhead. The results demonstrate a path toward practical, large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: The central challenge for large-scale quantum computing is suppressing errors, which requires error correction codes that balance encoding efficiency, error threshold, and hardware feasibility.
main_result: Cornucopia codes achieve an ultra-high encoding rate (>1/2) and a high pseudo-threshold ($\ge 0.4\%$) while maintaining low physical overhead suitable for near-term quantum processors.
method: The authors introduce Cornucopia codes, co-designing the code structure, physical layout, atom rearrangement protocol, and syndrome extraction schedule to enable parallel measurements.
model_or_system: The work is modeled using abstract qLDPC codes, specifically designed for implementation on reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays which provide long-range connectivity.
key_observables: Logical error rate ($p_L$), encoding rate ($r$), and physical overhead compared to established codes like the surface code or bivariate bicycle codes.
important_parameters: Physical error rate ($p=0.1\%$), logical qubit count (e.g., 1426), and circuit depth (constant for syndrome extraction).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a standard circuit-level noise model and relies on the feasibility of implementing coordinate permutations via global rigid motions in neutral-atom arrays.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate code block structures, geometric actions defining couplings, and the circuit scheduling for syndrome extraction across twelve layers. Tables compare performance metrics like logical error rates across different code families.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the trade-off limitations in existing codes to introducing Cornucopia codes. It details the hardware-aware co-design, analyzes the parallel syndrome measurement circuit, and mathematically proves the structure of the resulting logical error subspaces using group algebra homology.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete blueprint for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation by directly addressing hardware constraints (like connectivity and overhead) within the theoretical framework of QEC codes.
